title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a confirmatory, preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented agentic NetOps pipeline against an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). The study used gpt-5-mini as the generator (shared initial candidate), a deterministic NetOps validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) as the guard, and a preregistered paired design with N=400 tasks (800 episodes). Primary outcome: safe‑deploy (boolean) per episode. Results: complete pairs = 400; baseline (LLM‑only) successes = 400/400; guarded (verifier‑augmented) successes = 400/400; paired difference = 0.0; exact test p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Confirmatory conclusion: on this synthetic, constrained benchmark the verifier‑augmentation did not change the observed safe‑deploy rate. We interpret this null result conservatively: the benchmark produced a ceiling effect under the present model/validator/design rather than proving equivalence in broader operational settings. We report all preregistered artifacts, deterministic checks, and limitations; exploratory questions (canary sizing, failure‑mode clustering) remain relevant for future, harder benchmarks and runtime verifier integrations.

sections.introduction: Generative models and agentic LLM systems increasingly propose and execute NetOps changes (intent→configuration→action). Prior work shows LLMs can translate natural‑language intent to configuration artifacts and that verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair workflows can improve correctness in IaC and related domains. However, community reviews highlight evaluation gaps for action‑taking systems (lack of action‑aware benchmarks, limited production‑scale evidence). We designed a compact, reproducible paired experiment to test whether a deterministic verifier staged into an LLM agentic pipeline measurably improves end‑to‑end safety (safe‑deploy rate) compared with an LLM‑only agent under controlled, preregistered conditions. The paper (1) states the research question and preregistered hypotheses; (2) describes the benchmark, execution, and analysis; (3) reports the confirmatory results and deterministic reconciliation; and (4) interprets operational implications and threats to validity.
sections.related_work: LLM translation of operator intent to configurations has been demonstrated in prototype and benchmark settings (PreConfig; Intent→configuration studies) and in IaC work where verifier feedback improved correctness (TerraFormer). Deterministic network verification tools can detect reachability and configuration errors offline (MEV and related verifiers). Agentic, tool‑augmented LLM workflows (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestrations) show practical gains for AIOps/RCA but introduce new failure modes (hallucination, inappropriate tool calls) that guardrails aim to mitigate. Reviews highlight security/evaluation gaps for retrieval‑augmented and agentic systems and propose claim‑level calibration and verifier integration as promising directions. Our study builds on these findings by operationalizing a small, action‑aware staging benchmark and a preregistered paired test of a verifier loop versus an LLM‑only baseline.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered (study_id cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1). Primary research question: Can a compact action‑aware benchmark detect a higher safe‑deploy rate for a verifier‑augmented agent versus an LLM‑only agent? Primary hypothesis H1: verifier‑augmented agent achieves higher safe‑deploy rate; estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Design: paired binary outcomes, exactly N=400 paired tasks generated deterministically by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 under fixed seeds. Each task was run twice (baseline = LLM‑only; guarded = verifier‑augmented) producing 800 episodes total. Models and runtime: gpt-5-mini produced a single shared initial candidate per task (shared_initial_generation stage); verifier was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 used to score/accept candidate configurations. Preregistered exclusion rules: deterministic three‑replay consistency checks per agent+simulator pair; reproducible infrastructure or simulator failures flagged and excluded from primary analysis. Analysis: permutation‑based paired test (implementation used exact McNemar where applicable), bootstrap CIs for secondary measures. All scripts, seeds, raw outputs, validator traces, and execution manifests were archived as artifacts.
sections.results: Execution summary: started 2026-08-29, completed 2026-08-29; planned episodes = 800; completed = 800; model_calls_used = 400 (shared initial generation per task). Deterministic checks: all three‑replay consistency checks passed; no episodes excluded. Confirmatory analysis (preregistered primary estimand): complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400; guarded_success_count = 400; contingency: n_11 = 400, n_10 = 0, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Paired difference = 0.0. Exact two‑sided McNemar p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI for difference = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, 10,000 resamples). Secondary and exploratory measures: no rollbacks occurred in either condition (no time‑to‑rollback distributions to compare); failure‑mode clustering was vacuous since no failures observed. All per‑task validator traces and provenance archives are included in the execution artifacts.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: The preregistered, confirmatory result is a null effect: under the present synthetic benchmark, model (gpt-5-mini), and deterministic validator configuration the verifier augmentation produced no measurable safety improvement because every shared initial candidate was accepted as safe in both conditions. This outcome is consistent with a ceiling effect—tasks, prompt framing, shared initial generation semantics, or validator permissiveness produced universally valid candidates given the generator used. Operational implications: (1) Demonstrating verifier benefit requires benchmarks that produce nontrivial failure opportunities (harder semantics, adversarial intent variants, heterogenous models); (2) runtime verifier integration must be evaluated under conditions that exercise its blocking/correction path (e.g., retrieval‑poisoned or adversarial prompts, multi‑model ensembles, noisy initial candidates); (3) single‑model, single‑validator paired designs can yield informative null results that guide benchmark hardening. Relation to prior work: our findings do not contradict evidence that verifiers and generate–validate–repair pipelines improve correctness in IaC and controlled settings; rather, they emphasize the need for action‑aware, provenance‑sensitive benchmarks that meaningfully stress the guardrail paths. Limitations and next steps: see Limitations section.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a fully preregistered, archived paired evaluation of a verifier‑augmented NetOps agent against an LLM‑only agent on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark. The confirmatory outcome showed no difference (both conditions achieved 100% safe‑deploy on N=400 paired tasks). The null result points to a ceiling effect in the present benchmark and motivates development of harder, adversarial, and production‑reflective benchmarks, richer model sets, and runtime verifier integration experiments. We release the preregistration, execution artifacts, validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support community replication and benchmark extension.

limitations: Benchmark hardness: tasks were synthetic and produced a ceiling effect (both conditions returned universally valid candidates), limiting ability to detect verifier benefit.
Model and scope: single generator (gpt-5-mini) and single deterministic validator were used; results do not generalize to other models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Shared candidate semantics: the experiment used a shared initial candidate per task rather than independent per‑condition generation; this design choice was preregistered but reduces variance in generator outputs across conditions.
Synthetic environment: the simulator and validator do not fully model production runtime uncertainties, telemetry noise, or adversarial intent; external validity to live networks is limited.
Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts that might trigger guardrail interventions were not exercised here and remain an open question.
Sample interpretation: a null (no difference) result here reflects the benchmark and experimental configuration, not proof of equivalence in broader NetOps deployments.
